clue.text: Phantom on the loose in Henry VIII's court

indicators.note: something on the loose runs wild, so the letters of the word before are set free and rearranged

explanation.surface: A ghost wanders free through the Tudor king's palace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the loose' rearranges PHANTOM. Hampton Court is the palace by the Thames that Henry VIII took over from Cardinal Wolsey.
explanation.definitionFit: Hampton is the palace Henry VIII made his royal residence, named with its full title as Hampton Court.

clue.text: Native American tribal leader to push off

parts.note: the Hopi are a Native American people of Arizona

indicators.note: the leader of the word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A Native American chief is told to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' takes the first letter of 'tribal'; 'to' is a link. Hop it is British slang for go away.
explanation.definitionFit: Hop it is an informal British command to go away, the same as telling someone to clear off.

clue.text: My entertaining foul and fair companion for 8

indicators.note: the outer word entertains the jumbled letters, holding them inside

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: foul weather is rough, so the words beside it are churned into a new order

explanation.surface: My partner, both foul and fair, is the castaway's friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foul' looks like an adjective set against 'fair', but it is the anagram signal; 'entertaining' is the container. The 8 refers to 8 Down, Defoe's castaway novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Man Friday is the islander who becomes the shipwrecked hero's servant and friend in Defoe's novel.

clue.text: Initially, Lawrence Brown comes to us with complaint

parts.note: T. E. Lawrence, Lawrence of Arabia, is known by his initials T.E.
tan is a shade of brown
taken as written

explanation.surface: First, Lawrence Brown visits us with an ailment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' does not take a first letter here: it asks for Lawrence's initials, as in T. E. Lawrence; 'comes to' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: Tetanus is a bacterial disease, and complaint is used here in its sense of an illness.

clue.text: Help for ailing production of Achilles in Avon theatre

indicators.note: a stage production rearranges the material, so the words that follow are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A medical aid comes from staging a Greek tragedy at a Stratford theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'production of' rearranges ACHILLES IN AVON THEATRE, all twenty-one letters. Stratford-upon-Avon is home to the Royal Shakespeare theatre, so the picture is a staging there.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's state health service gives free medical care to the sick.

clue.text: Filled in footmarks at Edgbaston

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follows, spanning their boundaries

explanation.surface: Someone has filled in the footprints left on the Edgbaston cricket pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to letters running across 'footmarks at Edgbaston'. Edgbaston is a Test cricket ground in Birmingham; 'Filled in' looks like one phrase, but 'Filled' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sated means having eaten your fill, so it matches filled up or satisfied.

clue.text: Prodigal poet?

definitions.meaning: a wasteful person who gets through money freely
Stephen ... was an English poet of the 1930s generation; the question mark flags a name

explanation.surface: Is this extravagant person a poet?
explanation.definitionFit: A spender wastes money as a prodigal does, and Stephen Spender was a well-known English poet.

clue.text: Treat wild fish

indicators.note: wild suggests unruly, so the letters of the word beside it are scattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: Feeding a special meal to a fish caught in the wild.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges TREAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A tetra is a small tropical freshwater fish popular in aquariums.

clue.text: Called in Dee to put out of order

indicators.note: the call goes inside the river name

parts.note: taken as written; the Dee is a river in Wales and England, and in Scotland
rang means telephoned, or called

explanation.surface: Someone phoned from the River Dee to say things were broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Called in Dee' reads like a phone call from Chester; the Dee is a river flowing through Wales and England.
explanation.definitionFit: To derange is to disturb the order or arrangement of something, or to disorder the mind.

clue.text: Steal cunning connoisseur's book

parts.note: to rob is to steal

indicators.note: a cunning arrangement is cleverly contrived, so the word beside it is rearranged

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Pinch a clever collector's volume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cunning' rearranges CONNOISSEUR (the 's adds no letter) into INSONCRUSOE.
explanation.definitionFit: Defoe's 1719 novel of a castaway is a famous book.

clue.text: Grape in container passed round

indicators.note: the container is passed round the little word, so it goes outside it

parts.note: a pot is a common container
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grape sits in a bowl that is handed round the table.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinot is a family of grape varieties, such as Pinot Noir and Pinot Grigio.

clue.text: We're toast, out of control in plane

indicators.note: letters out of control are thrown into disorder, so the two words before are rearranged

explanation.surface: A pilot cries that they are doomed as the aircraft spins out of control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of control' rearranges the letters of WERETOAST, the apostrophe ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-seater is a small aircraft built for pilot and one passenger, so it is an example of a plane.

clue.text: Hill dealing with city

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor
to be onto something is to be dealing with it, or on the case

explanation.surface: A hill is being dealt with by the city planners.
explanation.definitionFit: Toronto is the largest city in Canada, the capital of Ontario.

clue.text: Breath so taken when pub hosts lottery

indicators.note: the pub hosts the lottery, so holds it inside

parts.note: an inn is a pub
a draw is a lottery or raffle

explanation.surface: Everyone gasps when the local holds its prize draw.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is descriptive: a breath taken in this way, drawn inwards, is a gasp.
explanation.definitionFit: Indrawn describes air pulled into the lungs, so a breath taken in that manner is a gasp or inhalation.

clue.text: Bread of Heaven a novelty

indicators.note: the bread is made of letters taken from inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Calling the hymn Bread of Heaven a novelty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread of Heaven' is a famous Welsh hymn line, which disguises 'of' as part of a title; it actually points to letters inside 'Heaven a novelty'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nan, also spelt naan, is a flat leavened bread from South Asian cooking.

clue.text: Port does badly with it

indicators.note: done badly, the word is put together wrongly, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: it means sex appeal, abbreviated SA, so with it is SA

explanation.surface: A harbour town performs poorly, despite being fashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges DOES into ODES. 'It' is old slang for sex appeal, written SA; 'with it' looks like 'fashionable'.
explanation.definitionFit: Odessa is a major Black Sea seaport in Ukraine.

clue.text: See 4 Down
One to deconstruct a lucid American novel

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: deconstructing takes a thing apart, so the two words before are broken down and reassembled

parts.note: US is short for American, as in US forces

explanation.surface: A critic sets out to pull apart a clear American novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to deconstruct' rearranges A LUCID into CLAUDI.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Graves's historical work about a Roman emperor, written as his memoir, is a novel.

clue.text: Very steep costs? Heavens above!

definitions.meaning: prices that are extremely high are described as being up in the clouds
taken literally, the heavens are the upper air, high in the firmament

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in shock at outrageous prices.
explanation.definitionFit: Sky-high is the idiom for extremely expensive, and literally means up among the heavens.

clue.text: A way small cat's grabbed limelight

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

indicators.note: the cat grabs the road, holding it inside

parts.note: a tom is a male cat; the 's means 'has'
RD is short for road, a way

explanation.surface: A small cat has caught a path into the spotlight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grabbed' puts A RD inside TOM, after S. The 's of cat's stands for 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stardom is the fame of celebrity, the state of being in the public eye.

clue.text: Accuse everyone possessed of little devil?

parts.note: an imp is a little devil or mischievous child
each means every one

explanation.surface: Charging everyone with being possessed by a small demon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possessed of' is just a link, saying the first piece is held along with the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To impeach is to formally charge a public official with wrongdoing.

clue.text: That is year after old lover's return

indicators.note: the year is put after the other piece
the lover comes back the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a leman is an archaic word for a lover or sweetheart

explanation.surface: A year later, a former sweetheart comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' reverses the lover, and 'after' sets the year behind. Leman is an archaic word solvers may not know.
explanation.definitionFit: Namely introduces a specific example, just as the phrase that is (i.e.) does.

clue.text: Work hard to cut grass have I been dragged through a hedge?

definitions.text: have I been dragged through a hedge?

indicators.note: the work and hard cut into the grass, going inside it

parts.note: a mead is a meadow, a grassy field, in poetic use
op is short for opus, a work
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Tackling a mown meadow leaves someone looking dishevelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have you been dragged through a hedge backwards?' is a British jibe at messy hair, so the question defines someone with untidy hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A mophead is a person with a mass of unruly, shaggy hair, the look the jibe mocks.

clue.text: City keeping time and so on

indicators.note: the city keeps the time, holding it inside

parts.note: EC is the postcode area of the City of London

explanation.surface: A city maintains its timetable, and other things besides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' puts T inside EC, the postal district of the City, London's financial district.
explanation.definitionFit: Etc is short for et cetera, Latin for 'and the rest'.

clue.text: One taking control speaks for Roman general

indicators.note: speaks says the phrase is said out loud, and the spelling follows the sound

parts.note: someone who takes a firm hold is a gripper, and one is A

explanation.surface: A person seizing power addresses the troops on behalf of a Roman commander.
explanation.walkthrough: 'speaks' signals a homophone: 'a gripper' said in a British accent, with the final R silent, sounds like the general's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcus Agrippa was Augustus's leading general, victor at the battle of Actium.

clue.text: Scripture teacher given lift, one getting up

indicators.note: in a down entry, a lift lifts the letters upwards, so the pair is read from bottom to top

parts.note: RE is religious education, the school subject once called scripture
sir is how pupils address a male teacher

explanation.surface: The religion teacher got a ride, as someone was rising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given lift' reverses RESIR, as the entry runs upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A riser is someone who gets out of bed, as in an early riser.

clue.text: Delight at unusual admission of training university

indicators.note: the outer word admits the others, letting them inside

parts.note: rare means unusual
PT is physical training

explanation.surface: Joy at an uncommon place in a university training course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at' just links the definition to the wordplay; PT is the British school term for gym lessons.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapture is a state of intense joy or ecstasy.

clue.text: Chief backed by three men

indicators.note: backed says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A leader with the support of three of his men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' reverses letters found across 'three men'. EMEER is a variant spelling of emir.
explanation.definitionFit: An emeer, or emir, is a Muslim ruler or commander.

clue.text: Mad, sad, secret thinker

indicators.note: mad means crazy or deranged, so the letters of the next two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A list of a brooding philosopher's qualities: crazy, gloomy, secretive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' rearranges SAD and SECRET together. It looks like the first of three adjectives.
explanation.definitionFit: René Descartes was the French philosopher of 'I think, therefore I am'.

clue.text: Zola finds direction and distance

parts.note: E is east, a compass direction
a unit of length, 1,760 yards, standing for a distance

explanation.surface: Zola discovers which way to go and how far.
explanation.definitionFit: Émile Zola was the French novelist, so his first name is a fair stand-in for him.

clue.text: Month in advance

definitions.meaning: the third month of the year
to go forward steadily, as troops do on foot

explanation.surface: A month for moving forward.
explanation.definitionFit: March is the third calendar month, and to march is to proceed forward with steady steps.

clue.text: The ultimate consumer?

parts.note: ultimate looks like 'supreme', but it means the one at the very end of the chain, the person who finally uses a product

explanation.surface: Someone is hailed as the greatest shopper of all.
explanation.definitionFit: The end-user is the final buyer or user of a product, at the last link of the supply chain.
